content: Taiji (太極) represents a state of being that originates from Tao (道) and Wuji (無極). It is a state of absolute existence and infinite potential. According to the Tao Te Ching, Tao manifests as the One, which is Taiji. In a Taoist guidance text, this concept is elaborated further: from Tao came Taiji, which then divided into yin and yang, or the Two Aspects. Yin and yang subsequently split into the Four Realms, which then gave rise to the Five Elements (Wu Xing). From this process, the world was created. Taiji represents the state in which the world became comprehensible before its creation. Taiji can be equated with the concept of the One, Oneness, or Unity, as described in the Tao Te Ching. It is associated with the attainment of Unity (得一). Translated as the great ultimate, Taiji is understood as the ideal state of existence. Yin and yang symbolize the contrasting qualities inherent in reality and experience. For instance, light contrasts with darkness, and this contrast provides both with context and meaning. Taiji is not merely a catalog of all things and potentialities but rather a complex interconnection of all things in all possible contexts. This concept is often used to illustrate the doctrine of cosmological unity, emphasizing the interconnectedness of all existence through the dialectical interplay of yin and yang. In Western interpretations of Taoism, Taiji is sometimes conflated with the myriad things (萬物). However, Taiji is not limited to representing what exists; it also encompasses what has existed, what will exist, and what could potentially exist. Historically, the concept of Taiji first appeared in the Zhuangzi, highlighting its early significance in Taoism. It is also mentioned in the Xì Cí (Great Appendix) of the I Ching, a foundational Taoist text. During the Song Dynasty, when Confucianism re-emerged as Neo-Confucianism, it synthesized elements of Chinese Buddhism and Taoism. This synthesis drew upon metaphysical discussions from the Book of Changes, further integrating the concept of Taiji into Chinese philosophical thought.
